descriptor: A salamander that never grows up, keeping its feathery gills for life in the canals of Mexico City.

physical.fact: It can regrow lost limbs, its spinal cord, and even parts of its heart and brain without scarring.

range.summary: Found wild only in the remnant canals of Xochimilco and the wetlands of Chalco in southern Mexico City, all that is left of an ancient lake system.

population.unit: axolotls per km² in Xochimilco (survey density)

source.label: Contreras et al. 2009, Biological Conservation; UNAM Xochimilco census 2014

population.note: Densities come from net surveys of the canals, not full counts. Some reports date the middle survey to 2004. A new UNAM census began in 2024, and press reports in 2026 described wild axolotls as extremely hard to find.

threats.title: Water pollution
threats.detail: Treated and raw wastewater flowing into the canals degrades the water axolotls breathe through their gills.

threats.title: Invasive fish
threats.detail: Introduced carp and tilapia eat axolotl eggs and young and compete for food.

threats.title: Urban sprawl
threats.detail: Housing and tourism are replacing the chinampa farm islands and canals.

threats.title: Collection
threats.detail: Wild axolotls have long been caught for food, traditional medicine and the pet trade.

places.name: Xochimilco canals, Cuemanco
places.note: Boat trips pass chinampa refuges, though wild axolotls are almost never seen.

places.name: Anfibium, Museo del Axolote
places.note: Axolotl museum at Chapultepec Zoo, the easiest place to see one.

places.name: Lake Chalco
places.note: The second remaining wild site, a shallow wetland on the city's eastern edge.

sightings.tip: Breeding peaks in late winter, when axolotls are most active and surveys find the most animals. Wild sightings are very rare, so museums and refuge tours are the realistic option.

actions.title: Adopt a chinampa refuge
actions.detail: UNAM's AdoptAxolotl campaign funds canal biofilters and farmers who keep refuges clean.

actions.title: Never release pet axolotls
actions.detail: Captive animals can carry disease and dilute the genes of the last wild populations.

actions.title: Buy chinampa produce
actions.detail: Food grown with traditional, low-chemical methods keeps farmland and clean canals in use.

actions.title: Choose captive-bred pets only
actions.detail: Never buy animals taken from the wild.

regions.name: Xochimilco canals
regions.note: Canals between the chinampa farm islands are the axolotl's last main stronghold.

regions.name: San Gregorio Atlapulco
regions.note: Its canals are part of the Xochimilco Ramsar wetland, designated in 2004.

regions.name: Chinampa refuge
regions.note: In 2009 farmers and UNAM researchers screened a canal with wooden filters to make an axolotl refuge.

regions.name: Chapultepec Park lakes
regions.note: A third wild population was confirmed in the lakes of Chapultepec Park in 2010.

regions.name: Lake Chalco
regions.note: Lake Chalco was drained for farmland between 1896 and 1907.

regions.name: Chalco wetland
regions.note: Wetlands on the old Chalco lakebed still hold a few wild axolotls.

rangeHistory.note: Axolotls may once have lived in Lakes Texcoco and Zumpango too, but there are no firm records, so they are not shown.

summary.text: The axolotl is a species of mole salamander. It is neotenic, reaching sexual maturity without undergoing metamorphosis, and the adults remain fully aquatic with obvious external gills. Axolotls may be difficult to distinguish from the larval stage of other neotenic adult mole salamanders, in particular the tiger salamander, or other species such as mudpuppies.
